stances.claim: A president chooses his official family according to his personal standards for vetting who can best transform his thoughts and dreams into reality -- for this reason if for no other, incoming President Duterte deserves sufficient leeway in choosing his Cabinet; critics have been 'too picky,' undercutting choices before they even take their seats.

Duterte himself is 'unconventional and sui generis' -- so it is unsurprising that his Cabinet officials are similarly unconventional and sui generis (Dominguez, Bello, Yasay, Esperon, Aguirre, Medialdea, Tugade, Cusi, Panelo all have prior administration service or high-profile celebrity status, but what matters is Duterte's trust and belief in them).
stances.rhetorical_move: presidential-character framing (Cabinet selection reflects president's character)

stances.claim: Under the doctrine of qualified political agency, Cabinet members are 'alter egos' (extensions of himself) -- their acts are deemed the President's unless he rejects/alters them, they carry his mandate/commitments/governance, and ultimately 'Their success will be his success. Their failures will be his failures' -- making Cabinet performance a presidential-accountability matter.

Cabinet life is hard: intense trimedia scrutiny ('the freest in the world... microscopes and telescopes, cameras and recorders... headlined, columnized, broadcast, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked'), Commission on Appointments interrogation about public and private lives, constitutional bars on other office/employment/profession/business + conflict-of-interest, live-simply requirement with SALN disclosure of assets/liabilities/relatives -- making Cabinet positions a high-cost vocation.

Despite the costs, the credibility created by the peculiarities of the incoming administration's victory + its clarion call for radical change creates 'the perfect scenario for sincere and selfless public service' for 'the best and the brightest who have been wary of joining public service' -- and the 2016 electorate's gamble on Duterte as 'catalyst of real and meaningful change' makes this a 'profoundly hopeful electorate' whose trust rests on these chosen ones.

notable_anecdotes: The 'too picky' critic-characterization -- using a familiar conversational adjective to dismiss premature criticism without itemizing objections.
The 'sui generis' Latin tag repeatedly applied to both Duterte and his Cabinet -- used to claim conventional standards do not apply.

The doctrine-of-qualified-political-agency invocation: 'Under the doctrine of qualified political agency, their acts are deemed to be the acts of the President unless rejected or altered by him' -- using a doctrinal anchor to make Cabinet performance a presidential-accountability matter.
The success/failure binary: 'Their success will be his success. Their failures will be his failures' -- captured in two parallel five-word sentences.

The trimedia-scrutiny catalog: 'headlined, columnized, broadcast, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked' -- seven verbs spanning legacy and digital media, demonstrating CJ's social-media awareness in this 2016 era.

The iPad/iPhone digital-reference suggestion: 'They might as well carry with them copies of these documents or digitize them in their iPads or iPhones for instant reference' -- using brand-specific devices to physicalize CJ's adaptation to modern legal practice.
Peter Laurel's principled declination of the education portfolio due to family conflicts -- single named example illustrating the constitutional bars in operation.
The 'profoundly hopeful electorate' characterization -- using elevated language to dignify the voter base that gambled on Duterte despite 'news about his faults and shortcomings.'

The closing welcome: 'I welcome these chosen ones of incoming President Duterte. On their shoulders rest the people's trust that they will help him carry out his mandate to effect the meaningful change they long for.' -- a benevolent valediction extending CJ's measured optimism.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban defends President-elect Rodrigo Duterte's Cabinet selection prerogative -- 'a president chooses his official family according to his personal standards for vetting who can best help transform his thoughts and dreams into reality' -- and argues that incoming President Duterte deserves sufficient leeway because critics have been 'too picky,' undercutting choices before they take seats. Duterte himself is 'unconventional and sui generis,' so it is unsurprising that he selected Cabinet officials who are similarly unconventional and sui generis. Many named appointees -- Carlos 'Sonny' Dominguez, Silvestre Bello II, Perfecto Yasay Jr., Hermogenes Esperon, Vitaliano Aguirre II, Salvador Medialdea, Art Tugade, Alfonso Cusi, and Salvador Panelo -- have served in previous administrations or been involved in high-profile happenings. What matters critically is that Duterte trusts and believes in them; they are his 'alter egos' (extensions of himself), and under the doctrine of qualified political agency their acts are deemed the President's unless he rejects or alters them. 'Their success will be his success. Their failures will be his failures.' Duterte's unpredictable persona and unorthodox utterances catapulted him to landslide victory -- his political party and partisan alliances were less important than his persona, and his slogan 'change is coming' is laden with manifold unspoken but forceful promises. He wants Cabinet members like him: strong-willed, decisive, daring, transparent, unorthodox, and able to deliver on grand promises. CJ then itemizes the high vocational cost: from his earlier column (6/20/10), Cabinet members and families must forego privacy because 'our tri-media, the freest in the world, will use microscopes and telescopes, cameras and recorders to scrutinize the minutest details of their lives and careers. Daily, they will be headlined, columnized, broadcast, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked. Twenty-four hours a day, Cabinet members will be on call, not just by the President, but also by radio and TV reporters.' The Commission on Appointments confirmation 'is not a cakewalk either,' with interrogations sometimes used to 'horse-trade political and personal favors' and long-forgotten enemies surfacing slight indiscretions. The Constitution bars Cabinet members from any other office/employment, from practicing any profession or participating in business, and requires strict conflict-of-interest avoidance (Peter Laurel declined the education portfolio for this reason -- his family is deeply involved in education and business); they must live simply, disclose assets and liabilities, and list relatives by blood or affinity at term-start and annually. They should be familiar with the Constitution, Anti-Graft Law, Ethical Standards Law, and Administrative Code -- 'They might as well carry with them copies of these documents or digitize them in their iPads or iPhones for instant reference.' On a more positive note, the credibility created by the peculiarities of the incoming administration's victory + its clarion call for radical change creates the perfect scenario for 'the best and the brightest who have been wary of joining public service' to engage in 'sincere and selfless public service.' The 2016 elections encountered a 'disillusioned electorate' that deeply sought genuine change, willing to gamble on someone believed to be the answer 'even as news about his faults and shortcomings came out' -- making this 'a profoundly hopeful electorate.' CJ welcomes these chosen ones: 'On their shoulders rest the people's trust that they will help him carry out his mandate to effect the meaningful change they long for.'
